IUT4.Rem2_3_5.content: [Par] proves the Mordell conjecture over complex function fields by metric estimates of displacements under the fundamental group of the base. Question (F. Voloch, September 2015): can part of IUT give a proof of Mordell over number fields without Belyi maps, as used in Corollary 2.3 via [GenEll] Theorem 2.1? The author's answer, as far as he can see, is no. (i) Starting from the Schwarz lemma and Kobayashi distance ([Lang2] Chapter I): (PB1) Parshin's proof uses the holomorphic (Kobayashi, Schwarz-theoretic) geometry of a two-dimensional complete hyperbolic manifold, Bogomolov's the real analytic symplectic geometry of the upper half-plane acting on a universal cover of S^1; this gap parallels the arithmetically holomorphic [Falt] versus the arithmetically quasi-conformal IUT (Remark 2.3.3 (iii)), so expecting a new Mordell proof from IUT is called unnatural. (ii) (PB2) Parshin uses many holomorphic maps from the disc D, Bogomolov a fixed copy of D; (PB3) Parshin's method gives rough finiteness for any genus >= 2, Bogomolov's explicit inequalities for elliptic curves; (PB4) Bogomolov's estimates depend on unipotent elements or commutators, Parshin's are uniform in small elements. (iii) The Schwarz-theoretic geometry of D has a natural analogue in IUT via categories of localizations ([GeoAnbd], [AbsTopI], [AbsTopII]), culminating in Belyi cuspidalizations: Belyi maps play the role of arithmetic analytic continuation. Hence any search in IUT for a Mordell proof or an analogue of Parshin's proof appears to lead to some application of Belyi maps.
IUT4.Rem2_3_5.conclusion: A negative heuristic answer: within IUT, a proof of the Mordell conjecture over number fields avoiding Belyi maps does not appear possible to the author; supported by the contrasts (PB1) to (PB4) and the role of Belyi maps as arithmetic analytic continuation. Not a theorem.
obligations: Nothing to prove; the answer 'no' is the author's assessment, explicitly qualified 'as far as the author can see'.
ambiguities: Page 65: 'applied to obtained' is a misprint for 'applied to obtain'.

IUT4.Sec3.Universes.content: Setting of Section 3: ZFC-models (models of the nine Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms and choice); a Grothendieck universe V is a set that is transitive, contains N, and is closed under power sets, unions of members, and images of surjections from members onto subsets of V; a V-set is an element of V. The ZFC-models used are typically those of universes inside an ambient ZFC-model satisfying the existence axiom (dagger^G): every set lies in some universe (a ZFCG-model). Consequence proved on page 67: for any set-indexed family of universes V_i there is a universe V with V_i in V for all i (apply (dagger^G) to the set {V_i} and use transitivity), so infinite ascending chains V_0 in V_1 in ... in V exist, while the axiom of foundation forbids infinite descending chains. Every set-theoretic formula used is assumed absolute: its validity for sets in a universe V is the same relative to V and to any universe W with V in W.
explicit_hypotheses: an ambient ZFC-model satisfying the existence axiom (dagger^G)
IUT4.Sec3.Universes.conclusion: Definitions of ZFC-model, universe, V-set, ZFCG-model; the proposition that any set-indexed family of universes is contained (as elements) in one universe, hence infinite ascending chains of universes exist; the absoluteness convention for set-theoretic formulas.
external_dependencies: Drk: Chapter 1, sections 2 and 3; Chapter 3, Definition 4.2
obligations: The existence of ZFCG-models is not discussed; the paper defers to [Ffmn] and states that precise statements lie beyond its scope (page 68).
The absoluteness of every set-theoretic formula used is an assumption of the section, not verified for any particular formula.
ambiguities: Page 68: the absoluteness proviso is imposed globally on 'every set-theoretic formula that appears'; which formulas of Sections 1 to 2 or of IUT I to III are meant to satisfy it is not specified.

IUT4.Def3_1.content: Species: a 0-species is a collection of conditions on a set expressible in ZFC; a 1-species is a 0-species of morphisms together with composition; a species is a 0-species and a 1-species defining a category in every ZFC-model; specimens, i-smallness, species-isomorphisms, the category determined by a species, model-free use.
explicit_hypotheses: set-theoretic formulas are absolute in the sense stated on page 68 (validity unchanged between universes V in W)
(ii): a 0-species S_0; (iii): a 0-species S_0 and a 1-species S_1 acting on it
IUT4.Def3_1.conclusion: Definitions of (i) 0-species, collections of species-data, 0-specimens, 0-smallness; (ii) 1-species acting on a 0-species via formulas Phi_1 and Phi_{1o1} with unique composites, associativity and identities in every ZFC-model, 1-specimens, 1-smallness; (iii) species, species-objects and species-morphisms, i-smallness, species-isomorphisms and automorphisms, model-free specimens; (iv) the category determined by a species in a ZFC-model.
obligations: A definition: nothing to prove. Species are not formalized.

IUT4.Def3_1.i.content: A 0-species S_0 is a collection of conditions given by a set-theoretic formula Phi_0(E) in an ordered collection E = (E_1, ..., E_{n_0}) of indeterminate sets, n_0 >= 1 (a collection of species-data). A 0-specimen is a specific n_0-tuple E of sets in some specific ZFC-model satisfying Phi_0(E), written E in S_0. S_0 is 0-small if in every ZFC-model its 0-specimens form a set.
explicit_hypotheses: Phi_0 a set-theoretic formula (absolute in the sense of page 68)
obligations: A definition: nothing to prove. Species are not formalized.
ambiguities: Page 68: a 0-specimen lives in 'some specific ZFC-model'; the definition does not fix how specimens in different ZFC-models are compared except through model-free specimens of (iii).

IUT4.Def3_1.ii.content: A 1-species S_1 acting on a 0-species S_0 is a pair of set-theoretic formulas: (a) Phi_1(E, E', F) in two collections of species-data E, E' for S_0 and an n_1-tuple F of indeterminate sets (written F : E -> E'); a 1-specimen is a triple (E, E', F) in a ZFC-model satisfying Phi_1, with domain E and codomain E'; (b) Phi_{1o1}(E, E', E'', F, F', F'') defining F'' as a composite of F with F'. Required in every ZFC-model: (c) any two composable 1-specimens have a unique composite; (d) composition is associative; (e) every 0-specimen E has a (necessarily unique) identity 1-specimen id_E that is a two-sided unit for composition. S_1 is 1-small if in every ZFC-model the 1-specimens E -> E' between two given 0-specimens form a set.
IUT4.Def3_1.ii.conclusion: Definitions of 1-species acting on S_0, 1-specimen, domain, codomain, composite (with existence, uniqueness, associativity, identities required in each ZFC-model), 1-small.
obligations: A definition: nothing to prove. Species are not formalized.
ambiguities: Page 69: the identity 1-specimen is said to be necessarily unique; this follows from (e) in the usual way.

IUT4.Def3_1.iii.content: A species S = (S_0, S_1) is a 0-species with a 1-species acting on it. i-specimens of S are i-specimens of S_i; 0-specimens are species-objects and 1-specimens species-morphisms; S is i-small if S_i is. A species-morphism F : E -> E' is a species-isomorphism if there is F' : E' -> E with both composites identities (E, E' are then species-isomorphic); a species-automorphism has equal domain and codomain. A model-free i-specimen is one given by a set-theoretic formula that determines the same i-specimen relative to the ZFC-models of V_1 and V_2 whenever V_1 in V_2 are universes of some ZFC-model.
explicit_hypotheses: S_0 a 0-species and S_1 a 1-species acting on it
IUT4.Def3_1.iii.conclusion: Definitions of species, species-object, species-morphism, i-small, species-isomorphism, species-isomorphic, species-automorphism, model-free specimen; the observation that composites of species-isomorphisms are species-isomorphisms (stated as immediate).
obligations: A definition: nothing to prove, except the stated observation on composites of species-isomorphisms. Species are not formalized.

IUT4.Def3_1.iv.content: The category determined by a species S in a ZFC-model has the species-objects of S in that model as objects and its species-morphisms as arrows; the paper notes that this description does determine a category.
explicit_hypotheses: S a species; a fixed ZFC-model
IUT4.Def3_1.iv.conclusion: Definition of the category determined by S in a ZFC-model, with the assertion (immediate from (ii) (c), (d), (e)) that it is a category.
obligations: A definition: nothing to prove, except that the data form a category, which follows from (ii) (c), (d), (e). Species are not formalized.

IUT4.Rem3_1_1.content: Familiar descriptions of N (for instance [Drk] Chapter 2, Definitions 2.3, 2.9), Z, Q, Q_p or R yield species whose only species-morphisms are identities and which have a unique species-object in each ZFC-model. These differ from, for instance, the species of monoids isomorphic to N with monoid isomorphisms, which has many species-objects in any ZFC-model, all species-isomorphic. The set-theoretic formula defining the former species N may be used to define a model-free species-object N of the latter species.
explicit_hypotheses: the descriptions of N, Z, Q, Q_p, R as set-theoretic formulas
IUT4.Rem3_1_1.conclusion: The species N, Z, Q, Q_p, R (with identity morphisms only) have exactly one species-object per ZFC-model; the species of monoids isomorphic to N has many species-objects, all species-isomorphic; the description of N gives a model-free species-object of the latter. Stated without proof.
obligations: Uniqueness of the species-object in each ZFC-model and model-freeness of the description of N are asserted, not checked.

IUT4.Rem3_1_2.content: (i) The essence of a species lies in its set-theoretic formulas (programs, software, a deterministic algorithm in a term suggested by Minhyong Kim), not in the sets occurring in particular ZFC-models. (ii) Analogy (from discussions with F. Kato): a fixed model of set theory is to the species-theoretic approach as varieties are to schemes, and as groups of specific matrices are to abstract groups; the category of a species in a ZFC-model is a specific representation of an abstract species. (iii) Identifying programs with the same output leads to an indeterminacy up to internal modifications of programs, with intractable problems beyond the scope of the paper.
IUT4.Rem3_1_2.conclusion: Heuristic explanation of the notion of species; no assertion needing proof.
obligations: Nothing to prove; an explanatory remark.

IUT4.Rem3_1_3.content: (i) The set-theoretic formulas of a species are usually not written out; they are those of the conventional descriptions of the objects, and one must check these are well defined and do not depend on arbitrary choices not describable by set-theoretic formulas. (ii) Data given by set-theoretic formulas carry a canonicality not shared by objects constructed using the axiom of choice in a particular ZFC-model; species thus let one measure the deviation of non-canonical objects from a canonical norm.
IUT4.Rem3_1_3.conclusion: A convention: the formulas are the conventional ones, subject to a well-definedness and choice-independence check by the reader; and a heuristic on canonicality.
obligations: The check that conventional descriptions are well defined and choice-free is delegated to the reader; it is not carried out for the species used in IUT.
ambiguities: Page 71: no criterion is given for when a construction counts as depending on 'arbitrary choices that are not describable via well-defined set-theoretic formulas'.

IUT4.Rem3_1_4.content: Since a species is given by set-theoretic formulas, the notion it defines is unaffected by extensions of the universe, such as the ascending chain V_0 in V_1 in ... in V of page 67. This is the sense of the term inter-universal: inter-universal geometry relates geometries occurring in distinct universes.
explicit_hypotheses: set-theoretic formulas absolute in the sense of page 68
IUT4.Rem3_1_4.conclusion: A species is immune to extensions of the universe; this explains the term 'inter-universal'. The immunity rests on the absoluteness convention of page 68.
obligations: The immunity is a consequence of the absoluteness assumption of page 68, not proved independently.

IUT4.Rem3_1_5.content: Remarks 3.1.2, 3.1.3, 3.1.4 apply equally to mutations, morphisms of mutations, mutation-histories, observables and cores (Definition 3.3).
IUT4.Rem3_1_5.conclusion: The remarks on set-theoretic formulas extend to the notions of Definition 3.3.
obligations: Nothing to prove.

IUT4.Ex3_2.content: Small categories, with isomorphism classes of covariant functors as morphisms, form a species: a category as a set of arrows with composition relations satisfying properties; a functor as the graph of its map on arrows; an isomorphism class of functors as a collection of such graphs. Dictionaries: 0-species with the notion of category, 1-species with the notion of isomorphism class of functors; 0-specimen with a particular small category, 1-specimen with a particular isomorphism class of functors.
explicit_hypotheses: small categories; covariant functors considered up to isomorphism
IUT4.Ex3_2.conclusion: The notions of small category and isomorphism class of functors form a species, and species-isomorphisms between its species-objects correspond to isomorphism classes of equivalences of categories (stated as easily verified).
obligations: The set-theoretic formulas are not written out; that composition of isomorphism classes of functors is well defined and that species-isomorphisms are exactly isomorphism classes of equivalences is asserted as easily verified.
ambiguities: Page 72: the sentence speaks of 'species-isomorphisms between 0-species'; it is read as species-isomorphisms between species-objects (0-specimens), i.e. between categories.

IUT4.Rem3_2_1.content: In Example 3.2 one could define 2-species and 2-specimens using isomorphisms of functors and take functors (not isomorphism classes) as the 1-species, and more generally n-species for n >= 1; this is not done because it would add unnecessary complexity, so functors are taken up to isomorphism.
IUT4.Rem3_2_1.conclusion: A design choice: species are truncated at level 1, with functors up to isomorphism; higher n-species are possible but not used.
obligations: Nothing to prove.

IUT4.Def3_3.content: Mutations between species S, S': set-theoretic formulas Psi_0, Psi_1 assigning to each specimen of S a unique specimen of S', compatible with composites and identities (so a functor in every ZFC-model); morphisms of mutations (natural transformations), isomorphisms, mutation-equivalences and quasi-inverses; mutation-histories indexed by oriented graphs; covariant and contravariant observables of a mutation-history over a simply connected graph, and cores.
explicit_hypotheses: S = (S_0, S_1) and S' = (S'_0, S'_1) species (Definition 3.1)
(iii): a mutation M : S ~> S'; for the bijection statement, S and S' 1-small
(iv): an oriented graph (underlying graph with a total order on the branches of each edge)
(v): a mutation-history H whose underlying graph is simply connected, and a species S'
IUT4.Def3_3.conclusion: Definitions of mutations, composition and identity mutations, morphisms and isomorphisms of mutations, mutation-equivalences (with the observation that for 1-small species they induce bijections on species-morphisms and species-isomorphisms), mutation-histories, observables and cores.
obligations: A definition: nothing to prove, except the observation in (iii). Mutations are not formalized.

IUT4.Def3_3.i.content: A mutation M : S ~> S' between species is a pair of set-theoretic formulas: (a) Psi_0(E, E') in species-data for S_0 and S'_0, such that for each E in S_0 in a ZFC-model there is a unique E' in S'_0 with Psi_0(E, E'), written M(E); (b) Psi_1(E, E', F, F') such that for each species-morphism F : E -> E' of S there is a unique F' : M(E) -> M(E') of S' with Psi_1, written M(F); F -> M(F) must respect composites and identities. In a fixed ZFC-model, M determines a functor between the categories determined by S and S'. Composition and identity mutations are evident.
IUT4.Def3_3.i.conclusion: Definition of mutation, with the consequence that in each ZFC-model a mutation gives a functor; composition and identity mutations.
obligations: A definition; that M is a functor in each ZFC-model is immediate. Mutations are not formalized.

IUT4.Def3_3.ii.content: A morphism of mutations Z : M -> M' (M, M' : S ~> S') is a set-theoretic formula Xi(E, F') such that for each species-object E of S there is a unique F' : M(E) -> M'(E) of S' with Xi, written Z(E), and for every species-morphism F : E_1 -> E_2 of S, M'(F) o Z(E_1) = Z(E_2) o M(F). In a fixed ZFC-model this is a natural transformation. Composition and identities are evident. Z is an isomorphism of mutations if every Z(E) is a species-isomorphism; equivalently (verified immediately) Z has a two-sided inverse morphism of mutations.
IUT4.Def3_3.ii.conclusion: Definitions of morphism of mutations, its composition and identities, isomorphism of mutations, with the assertion that Z is an isomorphism iff it has an inverse morphism of mutations.
obligations: The equivalence 'isomorphism of mutations iff invertible' is stated as immediate; not formalized.

IUT4.Def3_3.iii.content: A mutation M : S ~> S' is a mutation-equivalence if there is M' : S' ~> S with isomorphisms of mutations M o M' -> id and M' o M -> id; M, M' are then mutation-quasi-inverses. If S and S' are 1-small, a mutation-equivalence induces, for any two species-objects of S, a bijection between the species-morphisms (respectively species-isomorphisms) between them and those between their images in S'.
explicit_hypotheses: M : S ~> S' a mutation; for the bijection, S and S' 1-small
IUT4.Def3_3.iii.conclusion: Definition of mutation-equivalence and mutation-quasi-inverse; the observation that for 1-small species a mutation-equivalence is fully faithful on species-morphisms and on species-isomorphisms.
obligations: The bijection for 1-small species is stated without proof (it is the usual full faithfulness of an equivalence); not formalized.
ambiguities: Page 74: the bijection is asserted for 1-small species; the paper does not say whether 1-smallness is needed for the bijection itself or only for the morphisms to form sets.

IUT4.Def3_3.iv.content: An oriented graph is a graph Gamma (its underlying graph) with a total order on the two-element set of branches of each edge ([AbsTopIII] section 0). A mutation-history H = (Gamma, S*, M*) indexed by an oriented graph assigns a species S^v to each vertex v and a mutation M^e : S^{v_1} ~> S^{v_2} to each edge e from v_1 to v_2; it is a species-theoretic version of a diagram of categories ([AbsTopIII] Definition 3.5 (i)).
IUT4.Def3_3.iv.conclusion: Definitions of oriented graph and mutation-history.
obligations: A definition: nothing to prove.

IUT4.Def3_3.v.content: For a mutation-history H with simply connected underlying graph and a species S', a covariant (respectively contravariant) S'-valued observable V of H consists of observation mutations V^v : S^v ~> S' for each vertex and, for each edge e from v_1 to v_2, a morphism of mutations V^e : V^{v_1} -> V^{v_2} o M^e (respectively V^e : V^{v_2} o M^e -> V^{v_1}). A covariant observable all of whose V^e are isomorphisms of mutations is a core; being a core is called coricity. These are simplified species-theoretic versions of the observables and cores of [AbsTopIII] Definition 3.5 (iii).
explicit_hypotheses: H = (Gamma, S*, M*) a mutation-history whose underlying graph is simply connected
IUT4.Def3_3.v.conclusion: Definitions of covariant and contravariant observables, cores, coricity.
obligations: A definition: nothing to prove.
ambiguities: Page 74: the definition assumes the underlying graph simply connected 'for simplicity'; observables on graphs with loops are not defined.
Page 74: in the covariant case the morphism V^e runs V^{v_1} -> V^{v_2} o M^e, so a core identifies V^{v_1} with V^{v_2} o M^e up to isomorphism along every edge.

IUT4.Rem3_3_1.content: (i) The axiom of foundation forbids membership loops a in b in c in ... in a, yet one often wishes to identify objects at higher and lower levels of the membership structure; sets and bijections allow this, and species extend it: species-isomorphisms between species-objects at different levels simulate membership loops without violating foundation, typically identifying output species-objects with input species-objects of a mutation-history ... ~> S ~> S' ~> S'' ~> ... ~> S ~> .... (ii) The simpler the species, the easier to build loops; hence categories (Example 3.2) are preferred to schemes, a principal motivation for the geometry of categories and absolute anabelian geometry ([MnLg], [SemiAnbd], [Cusp], [FrdI]), for instance reconstruction of the underlying scheme in [MnLg] via Definition 1.1 (iv), and slim exponentiation in the Appendix to [FrdI]. (iii) It is also of interest to consider the portions left unaltered by the mutations, hence cores; cores allow one to describe, by non-coric observables, the altered portions in terms of the unaltered ones (cf. Remark 3.6.1 (ii)).
IUT4.Rem3_3_1.conclusion: Heuristic motivation of species, mutation-histories and cores; no assertion needing proof.
obligations: Nothing to prove; an explanatory remark.

IUT4.Rem3_3_2.content: A naive original motivation: local systems on a scheme need not be valued in modules over a finite ring; one may take local systems of schemes (the Galois mantle of [pTeich]) or of more general collections of objects, then local systems on their fibers, and so on, leading to systems of nested local systems. This underlies successive iteration of a mutation-history; viewing such iterates as an abstraction of nested local systems, a core is an object invariant under the operations producing them.
IUT4.Rem3_3_2.conclusion: Heuristic motivation of iterated mutation-histories and cores; no assertion needing proof.
obligations: Nothing to prove; an explanatory remark.
ambiguities: Page 76: 'successive iteration of a given mutation-history' is used but not defined in Definition 3.3.

IUT4.Ex3_4.content: (i) Topological spaces with continuous maps form a species S^top; universal coverings Xt -> X of pathwise connected spaces with compatible pairs of continuous maps considered up to deck transformations of the target covering form a species S^{u-top}, whose species-morphisms are, set-theoretically, collections of continuous maps differing by deck transformations. (ii) Groups with outer homomorphisms (homomorphisms up to inner automorphisms of the codomain) form a species S^gp, whose species-morphisms are collections of homomorphisms differing by inner automorphisms. (iii) The assignment (Xt -> X) -> Aut(Xt/X) (the deck transformation group) is a mutation S^{u-top} ~> S^gp: the fundamental group is a mutation.
explicit_hypotheses: (i): pathwise connected topological spaces with universal coverings
IUT4.Ex3_4.conclusion: (i) S^top and S^{u-top} are species; (ii) S^gp is a species; (iii) Xt -> X maps to Aut(Xt/X) is a mutation S^{u-top} ~> S^gp. All stated as easily verified, with the set-theoretic formulas left to the reader.
obligations: The set-theoretic formulas and the verification that (iii) respects composites and identities (an outer homomorphism of deck groups for each morphism of coverings up to deck transformations) are left to the reader.

IUT4.Ex3_5.content: (i) For a class S of connected normal schemes closed under isomorphism, with a set E_S describable by a set-theoretic formula containing a representative of every isomorphism class, universal pro-finite etale coverings of schemes in S with isomorphisms up to deck transformations form a species S^S. (ii) Likewise, for a class G of topological groups closed under isomorphism with such a set E_G, the groups of G with bicontinuous outer isomorphisms form a species S^G. (iii) For suitable G, deck transformation groups give a mutation Pi : S^S ~> S^G; the schemes of S may be called [absolute] anabelian if one specifies a mutation A : S^G ~> S^S that is a mutation-quasi-inverse of Pi. The existence of the bijections (full faithfulness) of Definition 3.3 (iii) is essentially the usual definition of anabelian; the species-theoretic approach formulates the algorithmic approach of [AbsTopI]. (iv) One must specify which species one works with: a profinite group merely as a profinite group differs substantially from the same group equipped with data from its construction as an etale fundamental group; this issue was a motivation for the theory of species.
explicit_hypotheses: (i): S a class of connected normal schemes closed under isomorphism, with a set E_S given by a set-theoretic formula meeting every isomorphism class
(ii): G a class of topological groups closed under isomorphism, with a set E_G given by a set-theoretic formula meeting every isomorphism class
IUT4.Ex3_5.conclusion: (i) S^S and (ii) S^G are species; (iii) Pi : S^S ~> S^G is a mutation, and 'anabelian' is defined by the specification of a mutation-quasi-inverse A of Pi; (iv) a heuristic on specifying species.
obligations: (i) to (iii) are stated as easily verified; the 'appropriate choice of G' in (iii) is not specified.
No anabelian result is proved here; (iii) is a definition.
ambiguities: Page 77, (iii): 'an appropriate choice of G' is left unspecified; it must at least contain the deck groups of the coverings in S.

IUT4.Ex3_6.content: (i) For a prime p and a reduced scheme S over F_p, S^(p) has the topological space of S and structure sheaf O_S^p; the inclusion gives Phi_S : S -> S^(p), and p-th powers give a natural isomorphism alpha_S : S^(p) -> S with alpha_S o Phi_S the Frobenius of S. S^{p-sch} is the species of reduced quasi-compact schemes over F_p with quasi-compact morphisms. The small etale site S_et has as objects etale morphisms of finite presentation T -> S equipped with a finite open cover {U_i} of S and factorizations T|_{U_i} in A^{N_i}_{U_i} -> U_i exhibiting finitely presented subschemes (every such T admits these data), and S-morphisms as arrows. S -> S_et is contravariantly functorial and given by set-theoretic formulas, giving the etale site mutation M^et : S^{p-sch} ~> S^cat (S^cat: categories with isomorphism classes of contravariant functors). The perfection S^pf (inverse limit of iterated Frobenius) with beta_S : S^pf -> S gives the perfection mutation M^pf : S^{p-sch} ~> S^{p-sch}. (ii) The Frobenius mutation F^{p-sch} : S -> S^(p) defines the Frobenius mutation-history ... ~> S^{p-sch} ~> S^{p-sch} ~> ...; invariance of the etale site under Frobenius ([FK] Chapter I, Proposition 3.16) says M^et exhibits S^cat as a core; M^pf also gives a core; Phi_S is a covariant observable with identity observation mutations, non-coric since Phi_S is not in general an isomorphism; beta_S is a morphism of mutations M^pf -> id relating it to the coric observable of M^pf. (iii) For torsion-free abelian monoids S^mon, M -> M^(p) = p M is the monoid-Frobenius mutation F^mon, with monoid-Frobenius mutation-history and a non-coric contravariant observable given by the inclusions M^(p) -> M; the p-perfection M^pf (inductive limit of multiplication by p) gives a core M^{pf-mon}, and M -> M^pf is a morphism of mutations id -> M^{pf-mon} relating the two.
explicit_hypotheses: (i): p a prime; S a reduced scheme over F_p; for the species S^{p-sch}, reduced quasi-compact schemes over F_p and quasi-compact morphisms
(iii): S^mon the species of torsion-free abelian monoids and monoid morphisms
IUT4.Ex3_6.conclusion: (i) Definitions of S^(p), Phi_S, alpha_S, S_et and the mutations M^et, M^pf; (ii) by [FK] Chapter I, Proposition 3.16, M^et is a core of the Frobenius mutation-history, M^pf is a core, Phi_S is a non-coric covariant observable related to M^pf by beta_S; (iii) the monoid analogue, with a non-coric contravariant observable and the core M^{pf-mon}.
obligations: That S -> S_et and S -> S^pf are given by set-theoretic formulas and are functorial is asserted; the coricity of M^et rests on [FK] Chapter I, Proposition 3.16, and the coricity of M^pf and M^{pf-mon} on the evident identifications S^pf = (S^(p))^pf, which are not written out.
(iii) for log schemes is left to the reader.
ambiguities: Page 79: the core of (ii) requires the observation mutations along the Frobenius mutation-history to be related by isomorphisms of mutations M^et -> M^et o F^{p-sch}; the paper does not specify the direction or the isomorphism (the comparison S_et with (S^(p))_et via Phi_S).
Page 79: the Frobenius mutation-history is indexed by an infinite chain, whose underlying graph is simply connected as Definition 3.3 (v) requires.
Page 80: 'an non-coric observable' is a misprint for 'a non-coric observable'.

IUT4.Rem3_6_1.content: (i) Example 3.6 gives a species-theoretic interpretation, via coric versus non-coric observables, of the difference between etale-type and Frobenius-type structures ([FrdI] section I4); the mutation-histories and cores of Example 3.6 (ii), (iii) are the motivating examples for the vertical lines (log-links) and horizontal lines (Theta-links of various kinds) of the log-theta-lattice ([IUTchIII] Definitions 1.4, 3.8), and for observables and cores in [AbsTopIII] Definition 3.5 (iii). (ii) Example 3.6 illustrates describing non-coric data in terms of coric data (beta_S, M -> M^pf); in the log-theta-lattice this appears in the vertically coric log-shells receiving the log-Kummer correspondences ([IUTchIII] Theorem 3.11 (ii)) and in the multiradial representations of [IUTchIII] Theorem 3.11 (i), which describe the arithmetic holomorphic structure on one vertical line relative to an alien one on another.
IUT4.Rem3_6_1.conclusion: Heuristic: Example 3.6 motivates the vertical and horizontal lines of the log-theta-lattice and the description of non-coric data by coric data in IUT III Theorem 3.11; no assertion needing proof.
obligations: Nothing to prove; an explanatory remark.

IUT4.Rem3_6_2.content: (i) Coric descriptions of non-coric data must use set-theoretic formulas: descriptions using arbitrary choices depending on a model of set theory do not allow one to calculate, within one universe, operations performed in an alien universe, as happens for the arrows of the log-theta-lattice, where distinct universes arise from distinct scheme-theoretic basepoints of ring theories not related by ring homomorphisms; this need led to inter-universal Teichmueller theory. The algorithmic approach (as opposed to a fully faithful, Grothendieck conjecture style approach, Example 3.5 (iii)) is essential, since only specific algorithms reveal relations between components, e.g. the cyclotomic rigidity isomorphisms behind Theta^{x mu}_LGP-link compatibility ([IUTchIII] Theorem 3.11 (iii) (c), (d)). (ii) The algorithmic approach of the series ([FrdI], [EtTh], [AbsTopIII]) was conceived in the spirit of species; the formulas are left implicit and the reader must check that conventional descriptions are well defined and choice-free. (iii) Cataloguing the possibilities arising from choices leads to sets of very large cardinality built by set-theoretic exponentiation (E -> 2^E), reminiscent of the growth of denominators when integrating an arbitrary connection in p-adic crystalline theory, as opposed to canonical connections and canonical liftings ([pOrd], [pTeich]), which may be liftings of minimal complexity ([Finot]).
IUT4.Rem3_6_2.conclusion: Heuristic: set-theoretic formulas and specific algorithms are needed to compare constructions across universes; the reader must check that the series' conventional descriptions are choice-free. No assertion needing proof.
obligations: Page 82, (ii): the verification that the conventional descriptions used throughout IUT are well defined and independent of arbitrary choices is explicitly left to the reader; this is an open obligation for any formalization of IUT I to III.

IUT4.Rem3_6_3.content: (i) The fundamental reason for inter-universality ([IUTchIII] Remarks 1.2.4, 1.4.2): etale fundamental groups (Galois groups) are automorphism groups of rings, which is incompatible with the vertical and horizontal arrows of the log-theta-lattice, as these do not arise from ring homomorphisms. Hence for v in V^non the only natural correspondence describable by set-theoretic formulas between the isomorphs of G_v on either side of a vertical or horizontal arrow is an indeterminate isomorphism of topological groups, and for Delta_v = Ker(Pi_v -> G_v) across a vertical (not horizontal) arrow an indeterminate isomorphism equipped with an outer action of G_v. (ii) For v in V^bad: (V1) across a vertical arrow the full arithmetic fundamental groups Pi_v are identified up to isomorphism; (H1) across a horizontal arrow only the G_v are identified and the Delta_v are distinguished. Reasons: (V2) constructing the log-link (the p_v-adic logarithm power series) needs the local ring structures, reconstructible only from the full Pi_v; (H2) constructing the Theta^{x mu}_gau, Theta^{x mu}_LGP, Theta^{x mu}_lgp-links, i.e. q -> {q^{j^2}}_{j = 1, ..., l*}, needs an isomorphism between objects depending on the labels j (built from Delta_v) and a label-free object q, possible only if the Delta_v on the two sides are kept distinct. The simultaneous realization of label-dependent and label-free objects in (H2) is likened to the vertical bicoricity of [IUTchIII] Theorem 1.5.
explicit_hypotheses: the notation of IUTchI Definition 3.1 (e), (f); v in V^non (for (i)) or v in V^bad (for (ii))
IUT4.Rem3_6_3.conclusion: Explanatory claims: (i) across arrows of the log-theta-lattice only indeterminate isomorphisms of G_v (and of Delta_v with outer action, across vertical arrows) are describable by set-theoretic formulas; (ii) (V1)/(V2) and (H1)/(H2) explain why vertical arrows identify Pi_v and horizontal arrows only G_v. Stated as consequences of the constructions of IUT I to III, not proved here.

obligations: The claims that the indeterminate isomorphisms are the only natural correspondences describable by set-theoretic formulas, and the necessity statements in (V2) and (H2), are asserted with references to IUT III; no proof is given here and none is formalized.
